label: Kindness and Compassion
framing: Kindness in Scripture is not mere niceness, a smoothing over of things. It is a strength that bends toward the weak, the active goodness of God himself, and Scripture says it is his kindness, not his thunder, that leads a hard heart to turn.
cultural: The Hebrew word often rendered kindness, hesed, named a loyal covenant love that held even when the other party deserved nothing, the steady mercy God shows his people across their failures. In the harsh economy of the ancient world, where the weak were left to fend for themselves, the law's command to leave the gleanings of the field for the poor and the stranger was kindness written into property itself. Compassion was not a feeling but an obligation owed to those with no claim of their own.
historical: The early Christians stunned the Roman world by nursing plague victims their own families had abandoned, and the emperor Julian, in the fourth century, complained that these Galileans cared for the empire's poor better than its own priests did. From Basil of Caesarea's hospital to the long tradition of Christian almshouses, the church built its kindness into stone and institution, treating mercy as something owed rather than merely felt.
application: Kindness is mostly small and unrecorded, the patient word, the unhurried attention, the help no one will know you gave. Look hardest at how you treat the people who can do nothing for you, the server, the stranger, the one already down. Let your kindness cost you something, since the kindness that costs nothing changes nothing. And remember that you have received a mercy you never earned, which is the only soil where real kindness grows.

verses.text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
verses.where: A worshiper asks what offering could satisfy God, thousands of rams or rivers of oil, and the prophet answers that God has already shown what is good: to act justly, to love mercy and to walk humbly with him. The site's note says the prophets attacked worship cut off from justice, though they did not abolish worship itself. Mercy here is something to love, not only to do now and then.

verses.text: But when a Samaritan on a journey came upon him, he looked at him and had compassion. He went to him and bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he put him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him. The next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper. ‘Take care of him,’ he said, ‘and on my return I will repay you for any additional expense.’
verses.where: A Samaritan sees the beaten man, has compassion, binds his wounds with oil and wine, brings him to an inn and pays for his care in advance. The site's note says he takes on open-ended responsibility for a stranger, and the plain note says the question becomes whose neighbour you are willing to be. The lawyer cannot bring himself to say the Samaritan; he says, the one who showed him mercy.

verses.text: Boaz replied, “I have been made fully aware of all you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband, how you left your father and mother and the land of your birth, and how you came to a people you did not know before. May the LORD repay your work, and may you receive a rich reward from the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have taken refuge.”
verses.where: Boaz tells Ruth, a foreigner gleaning in his field, that he has heard all she has done for her mother-in-law, and asks the LORD to reward her, under whose wings she has taken refuge. The site's note on the chapter says he protects her, feeds her and quietly tells his workers to leave extra grain for her. His kindness began with noticing, and much of it was done without her seeing.

verses.text: “Do not be afraid,” said David, “for surely I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will restore to you all the land of your grandfather Saul, and you will always eat at my table.”
verses.where: David seeks out Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, lame in both feet, tells him not to be afraid, restores his grandfather Saul's land, and gives him a place at the king's table for Jonathan's sake. The site's note gives two readings, one suspicious of David's motives and one that takes the narrator at his word that he is keeping faith with Jonathan. Either way, Mephibosheth ate at the king's table for the rest of his life.

verses.text: Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender.
verses.where: Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and he will repay the lender. The site's note says the chapter returns again and again to the poor, and that Proverbs never offers laziness as the only reason for poverty, naming injustice, oppression and plain misfortune as well. God counts what is given to the poor as given to him.

verses.text: A righteous man regards the life of his animal, but the tender mercies of the wicked are only cruelty.
verses.where: A righteous man regards the life of his animal, but the tender mercies of the wicked are only cruelty. The site's note lists care for animals among the chapter's subjects. Kindness reaches even to creatures that cannot thank anyone.

verses.text: Moved with compassion, Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man. “I am willing,” He said. “Be clean!”
verses.where: Moved with compassion, Jesus reaches out and touches the man with leprosy and says, I am willing; be clean. The site's note says that in touching an unclean person Jesus does not become unclean; the cleanness moves the other way. The plain note says the man doubted not Jesus' power but his wanting, and Jesus answered that first.

verses.text: The islanders showed us extraordinary kindness. They kindled a fire and welcomed all of us because it was raining and cold.
verses.where: After the shipwreck, the islanders of Malta show Paul's company extraordinary kindness, lighting a fire and welcoming them all because it was raining and cold. The site's plain note says they had no knowledge of Israel's God, and asks whether we have ever been surprised by the goodness of people outside our faith and thanked them. Kindness is something to receive humbly as well as to give.

verses.text: Or do you disregard the riches of His kindness, tolerance, and patience, not realizing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?
verses.where: Paul asks the one who judges others whether he despises the riches of God's kindness, tolerance and patience, not realizing that God's kindness leads him to repentance. The site's note says God's kindness is not indifference to sin but time given for repentance. Kindness, in God's hands, is how hard hearts are turned.

verses.text: But when the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind appeared, He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.
verses.where: Paul says that when the kindness and love of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not by righteous deeds we had done but according to his mercy. The site's plain note asks whether we remember what we were before grace found us, and how that changes the way we see others. All human kindness in Scripture answers a kindness that came first.

links.label: Practical guides for the inner life

misread.taken: Clothe yourselves with compassion and kindness, and forgive as the Lord forgave you, is used to tell a badly hurt person to act as if nothing happened, keep being nice, and go back to someone who is still hurting them.
misread.says: The site's plain note answers that question with a plain no. Forgiveness lets go of revenge; it is not the same as trusting someone again, and it does not mean a crime should go unreported or that anyone should stay in danger. A person can forgive and still keep a safe distance and tell the truth about what happened, and nothing in the passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger.
misread.text: Therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves with hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience. Bear with one another and forgive any complaint you may have against someone else. Forgive as the Lord forgave you.

whole: Kindness can sound small beside the great words of faith, a lesson for children. Yet most people can name the kind act that kept them going in a bad year: a meal left on a doorstep, a teacher who noticed, a stranger who stopped. Many of us are kind to people who can return it and short with those who cannot, gentle in public and sharp at home. Some confuse kindness with never saying anything hard, and others think being honest gives them the right to be unkind.

Scripture puts kindness much higher than that. Micah sums up what the LORD requires as acting justly, loving mercy and walking humbly with God. Paul says it is God's kindness that leads a person to repentance, and that the kindness and love of God our Savior appeared when he saved us, not by our deeds but by his mercy. Kindness in the Bible is first something God does, and only then something he asks. Part of why we are not kind is that we are tired; part is that we decide who deserves it. The lawyer in Luke wanted to know who counted as his neighbour, and Jesus answered with a Samaritan, a man the lawyer could not bring himself to name. Most of us have someone we were raised to look down on, and the parable makes that person the one who did right.

So the Bible's wisdom about kindness is practical. It notices, as Boaz noticed Ruth's loyalty and quietly told his workers to leave grain for her. It remembers old debts of love, as David looked for someone in Saul's house to whom he could show kindness for Jonathan's sake. It reaches the poor, since Proverbs calls kindness to them a loan to the LORD, and it reaches even an animal. It touches what others avoid, as Jesus touched the man with leprosy. And it receives kindness humbly, as Paul's shipwrecked company did from islanders who knew nothing of Israel's God. Kindness is not the same as having no limits: the site's plain note on Colossians 3 says that forgiving and bearing with one another never means staying where someone is hurting you, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

The hope Scripture gives is that every kindness we manage reflects one we first received. We were saved, Paul writes to Titus, not by the righteous things we had done but according to God's mercy, and the plain note says that a person who remembers what they were before grace found them sees others differently. The God who is gracious and compassionate does not run out, and the kindness he asks of us is drawn from his supply, not from ours.
deep.sit: Who is the person you find hardest to be kind to, and what is one kind thing, safe and wise, you could do for them this week?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says many people picture God as quick to anger and slow to forgive, and that verse 8 says the opposite, in the words God used to describe himself. Pray it, and ask to become like him.
prayer.text: The LORD is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion. The LORD is good to all; His compassion rests on all He has made.

careLines.text: Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
